name: Panax ginseng

card.summary: A classic East Asian adaptogen root sold for energy, libido and testosterone; a Cochrane review found small, likely not clinically meaningful effects on erectile function.
card.aka: Korean ginseng, Asian ginseng, red ginseng
card.note: Can interact with drugs such as warfarin; reported side effects include headache, insomnia and raised blood pressure.

quick.overview:
Panax ginseng is a perennial root herb from the Russian Far East, northeast China and Korea, central to traditional East Asian medicine as a tonic. It is processed as white or red ginseng and sold as capsules, extracts and drinks for energy, stress and sexual function.

In men with mild to moderate erectile dysfunction, a Cochrane review of nine placebo-controlled trials (587 men) found small improvements in erectile function that were likely not clinically meaningful, mostly on low-certainty evidence. Wikipedia states there is little evidence of a health effect.
quick.mechanism: The active constituents are thought to be ginsenosides, triterpene saponins that have been studied for effects on inflammation, vascular tone and nitric oxide signaling. Network-pharmacology and laboratory work proposes multiple targets; human mechanistic evidence is limited.
quick.risks: Wikipedia lists headache, raised blood pressure, diarrhea, insomnia and rash as common side effects, notes possible interactions with prescription drugs such as warfarin, and says use in pregnancy and breastfeeding is potentially unsafe.

lead: Panax ginseng, also called Asian, Chinese or Korean ginseng, is a perennial plant native to mountainous areas of the Russian Far East, northeast China and the Korean peninsula; its root is the original source of ginseng and is harvested after five or six years of cultivation [1]. It is used in folk and traditional medicine as a tonic [1][2].

In appearance and fitness communities and the wider supplement market it is sold for energy, stress, libido and testosterone support, and appears in multi-herb men's-health products [3]. Research has examined it for erectile dysfunction, fatigue, cognition and other outcomes. A Cochrane review concluded that effects on erectile function were small and probably not clinically meaningful, with mostly low-certainty evidence [4]. Wikipedia states there is little evidence that it provides any health effect, and that its constituents are under preliminary research [1].

Ginseng is grown mainly in South Korea, China, Canada and the United States, and the market is large: Wikipedia cites global sales above $2 billion in 2013, about half produced by South Korea [12]. The root is processed as white ginseng (peeled and dried) or red ginseng (steamed, then dried), and appears in capsules, extracts, teas, energy drinks and Korean foods such as chicken ginseng soup [12]. NCCIH describes it as a traditional calming agent and adaptogen, a term for substances said to help the body resist stress [11].

paras: Ginseng root is used in traditional East Asian medicine as a general tonic and is sold as capsules, extracts, teas and drinks. Modern marketing emphasizes fatigue, stress resilience, cognition and sexual function [1][2].

The Shennong Ben Cao Jing, an early Chinese materia medica attributed to around 196 AD, is among the first texts to discuss ginseng as medicine, and Li Shizhen's Compendium of Materia Medica (1596) called it a superior tonic used mainly in chronic illness and convalescence rather than as a cure-all [12]. In Korea the dried root is cooked into soups, brewed into insam-cha tea and steeped in liquor [12].

NCCIH lists stress, cognition, flu, fatigue, athletic performance, diabetes, aging, asthma and anxiety among the reasons people take Asian ginseng, and notes it is usually sold as a dietary supplement that is not approved by the FDA before sale [11]. Commercial labels for multi-herb vitality products containing Panax ginseng describe temporary relief of low energy and a run-down feeling [3]. Supplement marketers often cite its adaptogenic properties [12][13].

Lifters on forums such as T Nation sometimes list ginseng among stacks that also include zinc, maca or ginkgo, usually changed together with diet or training, which makes individual effects hard to separate.

A Cochrane systematic review of nine trials (587 men with mild to moderate erectile dysfunction) compared ginseng only with placebo over up to 12 weeks. Gains in erectile function were small and probably not clinically meaningful; men may report better ability to have intercourse; adverse events did not clearly differ; most evidence was low certainty; and no trial compared ginseng with PDE-5 inhibitors [4]. A 2024 randomized trial of 98 men tested a combination of ginseng, Tribulus terrestris and L-arginine versus placebo and reported improved IIEF-5 scores overall, with no significant benefit in men with diabetes [4].

ClinicalTrials.gov lists ginseng trials on fatigue and stress, cancer-related fatigue, cognition, bone metabolism and exercise-induced muscle soreness [6]. Studies of ginseng on testosterone are discussed in a 2021 systematic review of herbs, which reported some supporting evidence for Asian red ginseng but concluded evidence was limited [7].

NCCIH summarizes the research as follows: some small studies suggest improved attention and reaction time in middle-aged but not young adults; a 2023 review found a possible small benefit for general fatigue from ginseng alone; a 2022 review found improvements in cardiometabolic markers such as fasting glucose in people with prediabetes or diabetes, though blood sugar control in diabetes is inconclusive; and most research finds no improvement in athletic performance. NCCIH adds that most trials have been small, under 200 participants, and under three months long [11].

A 12-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial tested a sprout ginseng extract in people with subjective memory impairment [15]. A registered trial of ginseng for stress and fatigue enrolled 50 participants [6], and a small registered trial of American ginseng (a related species) examined exercise-induced muscle soreness in 10 participants [16].

Wikipedia reports that ginseng is generally considered safe for adults when used under six months, possibly unsafe longer, and lists headache, raised blood pressure, diarrhea, insomnia, rash and vaginal bleeding as side effects; it may interact with prescription drugs such as warfarin, and its use during pregnancy and breastfeeding is potentially unsafe [1]. Reviews of herb-drug interactions and perioperative care discuss ginseng among herbs that may affect bleeding and blood sugar [8][9].

NCCIH reports that insomnia is the most common side effect, with severe rash, liver damage and severe allergic reactions less common; ginseng may lower blood sugar, may worsen autoimmune disorders, and may interfere with blood clotting [11]. Topical safety has not been established and irritation or burning can occur [11]. Short-term oral use of up to six months appears safe for most people, while long-term safety is less clear [11]. An American Family Physician review also covers interactions and precautions [14].

The main bioactive constituents are ginsenosides, whose chemistry, biosynthesis and proposed effects on inflammation and the vascular system have been reviewed [5][10]. Pharmacology reviews describe multiple constituents with multiple, sometimes opposing, actions [10].

Ginsenosides fall into dammarane and oleanane skeleton types and occur almost exclusively in Panax species [5]. Reviews of their molecular mechanisms describe effects on inflammatory signalling and vascular function, largely from cell and animal work [17][18].

French Jesuit Pierre Jartoux described the plant in a 1711 letter, recording a Chinese name meaning form of man in reference to the root's shape [1]. It is protected in Russia and China, and most commercial supply comes from cultivation [1].

Jartoux's letter, dated 12 April 1711, was published in 1713 in the Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society [1]. Control of ginseng fields became an issue in China and Korea in the sixteenth century, and wild American ginseng was harvested for export from the mid-1700s [12]. Wild Korean ginseng, gathered by mountain foragers called simmani, is now rare, and most supply comes from cultivated fields; roots are usually harvested at five or six years [1][12].

In the United States ginseng is sold as a dietary supplement; Wikipedia notes that the FDA and the FTC have sent warning letters to supplement makers over unsupported health claims [12]. The plant is protected in Russia and China [1].
The adaptogen idea, reviewed in a 2021 historical article, groups substances said to raise resistance to physical and mental stress; Panax ginseng is among the plants most often named [13].

chain: Taken as a root extract or capsule
Marketed for energy, stress resilience and libido
Claimed to support training and day-to-day vitality
angle.text: People in fitness and men's-health circles take ginseng as a tonic they hope will raise energy and drive, so that they train and recover more consistently. Any link to appearance runs through that chain rather than through a direct effect on skin or physique.
